title: Going Prob'n

contributors.contribution: Created the original C.E.L.L. game's character, environment, and supporting visual artwork.
Helped develop the original C.E.L.L. version's comedic story, dialogue, character ideas, and voice material.
Created music and sound for the original C.E.L.L. version.

description: Going Prob'n began as a substantial C.E.L.L.-based action game built with my regular Square Particle collaborators. The player controls a UFO, abducts humans, converts civilians into zombies, destroys buildings, and uses absurd physics-style alien weapons while conquering cities, towns, farms, and military bases. I later revisited the same game in Unity for Android, moving the presentation into 3D, using real physics to expand the destruction and object-based weapons, and optimizing the city for mobile rendering.

sections.title: Project Status
paragraphs: This was a working unreleased side project rather than a commercially released game.
The prototype implemented substantial gameplay and systems, but development stopped before a production release.

sections.title: Original C.E.L.L. Game
paragraphs: Going Prob'n was originally developed on my C.E.L.L. cross-platform game-engine architecture.
The C.E.L.L. version established the game's core identity: side-view UFO gameplay, alien weapons, human abduction, zombie conversion, environmental destruction, world conquest, and the comedic story.

sections.title: C.E.L.L. Team Production
paragraphs: The original version was a four-person Square Particle collaboration.
I led the technical implementation and game design while working with my regular artist, story/voice collaborator, and audio contributor.
items: Artist: original character, environment, and game artwork
Story / voice contributor: narrative, character ideas, dialogue, and voice material

sections.title: The Premise
paragraphs: Going Prob'n followed two aliens who arrive on Earth convinced that their mission is to conquer it.
The comedy came from the fact that they had completely misunderstood their orders.

sections.title: Side-View UFO Gameplay
paragraphs: The core presentation had a Choplifter-like side-view structure, with the player piloting a UFO over populated environments.
The UFO could attack, abduct, manipulate physical objects, and interact with the world below.

sections.title: Abduction & Zombie Conversion
paragraphs: Humans could be abducted and converted into zombies.
Those zombies could then be used to attack other locations, turning captured civilians into part of the larger conquest loop.

sections.title: Physics-Style Alien Weapons
paragraphs: The weapon design focused on playful systemic interactions rather than only conventional projectiles.

sections.title: Tractor Beam Combat
paragraphs: The tractor beam could pick up objects such as cars and cows.
The player could swing captured objects beneath the UFO like pendulum weapons and use them against people, vehicles, or structures.

sections.title: Reverse-Gravity Bombs
paragraphs: Reverse-gravity attacks could launch people upward toward the UFO.
This worked both as crowd control and as an alternate way to abduct civilians.

sections.title: Destructible World
paragraphs: Buildings and environmental objects could be destroyed during normal play.
The destruction gave the game a Rampage-like sense of chaos while preserving the UFO-based control model.

sections.title: World Conquest
paragraphs: The design extended beyond one isolated level.
The larger game world included cities, towns, farmland, and military bases that the aliens could progressively attack and conquer.

sections.title: Comedic Story Payoff
paragraphs: The ending was written around the central misunderstanding.
After the protagonists proudly survey the destruction they caused, the rest of the alien armada arrives and reveals that they were actually supposed to save Earth.

sections.title: Later Unity / Android Remake
paragraphs: I later returned to Going Prob'n and began rebuilding it in Unity for Android.
This was an evolution of the same game rather than a separate project, so both generations belong on the same portfolio card.

sections.title: 3D Presentation
paragraphs: The Unity version moved the visual presentation toward 3D while preserving the original side-view UFO gameplay concept.

sections.title: Unity Physics
paragraphs: Unity's built-in physics made the game's destruction and object-based weapons much more dynamic.
Picking up, swinging, throwing, and blowing up objects became a much richer part of the gameplay.

sections.title: Android Draw-Call Optimization
paragraphs: The hardest technical problem in the Unity remake was rendering a large number of city buildings efficiently on contemporary Android hardware.
I reduced draw calls by sharing textures/materials across groups of buildings and combining meshes so the city could be rendered with far fewer submissions.

sections.title: Systemic Game Design
paragraphs: The game's strongest design idea was that the player's tools created unscripted moments.

A car could become a pendulum weapon, a crowd could be launched upward by reverse gravity, destroyed buildings could reshape the encounter, and abducted civilians could become units used against another location.

sections.title: Project Status
paragraphs: Going Prob'n did not reach commercial release, but the original C.E.L.L. version developed into a substantial team project with a defined story, world structure, and gameplay loop.
The later Unity/Android remake extended the same design into 3D physics and mobile-performance experimentation.

historicalNotes: Going Prob'n began as a C.E.L.L.-based Square Particle game and was later partially rebuilt in Unity for Android.
The four-person team applies to the original C.E.L.L. generation.
The original team consisted of Jamie plus his recurring artist, story/voice contributor, and audio contributor.
The later Unity/Android remake was a subsequent technical evolution of the same game.
The C.E.L.L. generation established the core side-view gameplay, comedy, alien weapons, abduction, zombie conversion, destruction, and world-conquest structure.
The Unity version moved the presentation into 3D and used Unity physics to expand physical interaction and destruction.
The Unity Android version required draw-call optimization because of the large number of background city buildings.
Jamie reduced draw calls through shared textures/materials and mesh combining.
Only partial source/material appears to survive, so public technical claims should remain grounded in direct memory and surviving media.
Going Prob'n is a substantial unreleased project and must remain outside the canonical six released-game count.
